title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
summary: The difference between renewable sources that naturally replenish, like sunlight, wind, and water, and nonrenewable sources, like oil, coal, and gas, that take millions of years to form.
poll: Countries should use more renewable energy, even if it costs more right now.

versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
All around us, things need power. Lights need it. Cars need it. Toys need it, too. This is energy.

There are two kinds. One kind never runs out. We call it renewable. The sun is this kind. Wind is this kind. Water is this kind, too.

The other kind can run out. We call it nonrenewable. Oil is this kind. Coal is this kind. Gas is this kind, too. These are fuels. They formed deep in the ground over millions of years. We can not make more soon.

Burning oil, coal, and gas can make the air bad. The sun, wind, and water keep the air clean.

Many lands use both kinds. Some day, more lands will use the kind that never runs out. This helps us all.

versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
All around us, things need power to work. Lights need it. Cars need it. Toys and clocks need it, too. This power is a kind of energy. It comes from somewhere.

There are two kinds of power. The first kind never runs out. We call it renewable. The sun is one kind. Wind is one kind. Moving water is one kind, too. The sun comes up each day. Wind keeps blowing.

The second kind can run out. We call it nonrenewable. Oil, coal, and gas are this kind. These are called fuels. They formed deep in the ground. It took millions of years. Once people use up this fuel, nobody can make more of it soon.

Burning oil, coal, and gas can make the air dirty. Using the sun, wind, and water makes the air much less dirty.

Today, many lands use a mix of both kinds of power. Slowly, more lands use more of the kind that never runs out. Knowing where power comes from helps us use it wisely.

versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
Almost everything around us needs power in order to work. Lights need it to shine, cars need it to move, and clocks and toys need it to run. This power is a kind of energy. Where does it come from?

There are two main kinds of power. The first kind comes from things that fill back up and do not run out. We call this renewable power. Sunlight, wind, and moving water are all like this. The sun rises again every day. Wind keeps blowing across the land. Rivers keep flowing toward the sea.

The second kind comes from things that can run out. We call this nonrenewable power. Oil, coal, and gas, often called fossil fuels, are the main examples. These fuels formed deep in the ground over millions of years, from the buried remains of old plants and animals. Once people use up a supply of oil, coal, or gas, nobody can make more of it soon.

Burning oil, coal, and gas to make power lets out gases that can make the air dirty. It can affect the planet's climate over time, too. Using sunlight, wind, and water to make power lets out far less of this kind of dirt.

Today, most lands around the world use a mix of both kinds of power. Slowly, more lands are choosing to add more of the kind that does not run out. Understanding where power comes from helps everyone use it wisely.

The second group, nonrenewable energy, includes oil, coal, and gas, often grouped as fossil fuels. versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
Almost everything in daily life depends on a steady, reliable supply of power. Lights need it to shine, cars need it to move, and tools and clocks need it to run. This power is energy, and not all of its sources are really the same.

Power sources generally fall into two groups. The first group, renewable energy, comes from things that naturally and continually replenish, and therefore almost never run out on a human timescale. Sunlight, wind, and flowing water are the most common renewable sources. The sun rises again every day, wind keeps circulating across the land, and rivers persistently flow toward the sea.

The second group, nonrenewable energy, includes oil, coal, and gas, often grouped under the term fossil fuels. These fuels formed deep underground over millions of years, as old plants and animals were gradually changed by heat and pressure. Because this takes such an extraordinarily long span of time, once a supply of oil, coal, or gas becomes fully used up, people cannot really produce new supplies within a single lifetime.

These two groups also differ in another significant way. Burning fossil fuels to make usable power releases gases that can pollute the air and gradually affect the climate over time. Making power from sunlight, wind, and water releases much less of this kind of dirt.

Today, the majority of lands rely on a mixture of both kinds of power at once, often in very different amounts. An increasing number of nations are gradually shifting toward using a considerably larger share of renewable sources every year. Understanding this difference helps citizens, engineers, and leaders make better choices about the future of power for everyone.

versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
Almost everything in daily life depends on a steady, reliable supply of power. Lights need it to shine, cars need it to move, and tools and machines need it to operate. Where does all of this power actually come from, and are all of its sources really the same?

Power sources fall into two broad groups. The first group, renewable energy, comes from things that naturally and continually replenish on a human timescale, and so are considered essentially inexhaustible. Sunlight, wind, and flowing water are the most common renewable sources. The sun rises again every single day, wind keeps circulating across the land, and rivers persistently flow toward the sea no matter how much power people capture from them.

The second group, nonrenewable energy, includes oil, coal, and gas, grouped together under the term fossil fuels. These finite fuels formed deep underground over millions of years, as old plants and animals were transformed by intense heat and geological pressure. Because this takes such an extraordinarily long span of time, once a supply of oil, coal, or gas becomes fully used up, people cannot realistically produce new supplies within a lifetime; the supply is, for practical purposes, fixed.

These two groups also differ in another significant way: burning fossil fuels to make usable power releases gases that pollute the air and gradually affect the climate, while making power from sunlight, wind, and water releases much less of this harmful dirt.

Today, most countries rely on a mix of both kinds of power, often in very different amounts. An increasing number of nations are working to diversify their supply and build a more sustainable mix by adding more renewable sources every year. Understanding this difference helps citizens, engineers, and leaders make better, more informed choices about the long-term future of power.

Power sources fall into two broad groups. versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
Almost everything in daily life depends on a steady, reliable supply of power; lights need it to shine, cars need it to move, and tools and machines need it to operate from moment to moment. Where does all of this power actually come from, and are all of its sources really the same, or do meaningful differences separate them?

Power sources generally fall into two broad groups. The first group, renewable energy, comes from sources that naturally and continually replenish on a human timescale, and so are considered essentially inexhaustible for all practical purposes. Sunlight, wind, and flowing water are the most common renewable sources, because the sun rises again every single day without fail, wind keeps circulating across the land, and rivers persistently flow toward the sea no matter how much power people capture from them.

The second group, nonrenewable energy, includes oil, coal, and natural gas, often grouped together under the term fossil fuels. These finite fuels formed deep underground over millions of years, as old plants and animals were gradually transformed by intense heat and geological pressure acting over almost unimaginable stretches of time. Because this takes such an extraordinarily long span of time, once a given supply of oil, coal, or gas becomes fully depleted, people cannot realistically produce meaningful new supplies within a single human lifetime; for all practical purposes, the supply is fixed and strictly finite.

These two groups also differ in another significant way: burning fossil fuels to make usable power releases gases that pollute the air and gradually affect the climate over time, whereas making power from sunlight, wind, and water releases substantially less of this harmful pollution, even when accounting for the resources needed to manufacture and install the equipment.

Today, the overwhelming majority of countries continue to rely on a mixture of both kinds of power, often in widely varying amounts. An increasing number of nations are gradually working to diversify their supply and build a considerably more sustainable mix by adding a larger share of renewable sources year after year. Understanding this difference helps citizens, engineers, and leaders make better, more carefully informed choices about the long-term future of power.

Humans have harnessed renewable energy for thousands of years, long before the modern term even existed. Ancient water wheels used the steady power of flowing rivers to grind grain into flour, and sailing ships harnessed the wind to cross oceans and seas, well before coal and oil became widely used fuels during the industrial era that began only a few centuries ago.

versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
Power sources that run modern daily life generally fall into two broad groups, and understanding the difference between them matters more today than ever before, as lights, cars, tools, and machines all depend on a continuous and reliable supply of power simply to operate.

The first group, renewable energy, comes from things that naturally and continually replenish on a human timescale, and these sources are therefore considered essentially inexhaustible for all practical purposes. Sunlight, wind, and flowing water are the most common renewable sources. The sun predictably rises again every single day without fail, wind keeps circulating across the land, and rivers persistently flow toward the sea no matter how much power people capture from them.

The second group, nonrenewable energy, includes oil, coal, and gas, grouped together under the term fossil fuels. These finite fuels formed deep underground over millions of years, as old plants and animals were transformed by intense heat and geological pressure acting over almost unimaginable stretches of time. Because this takes such an extraordinarily long span of time, once a supply of oil, coal, or gas becomes fully used up, people cannot realistically produce new supplies within a lifetime, so for all practical purposes, the supply is fixed and strictly finite.

A further distinction separates these two groups just as clearly: burning fossil fuels to make usable power releases gases that pollute the air and gradually affect the climate, whereas making power from sunlight, wind, and water releases much less of this harmful dirt, even counting the resources needed to build and install the equipment.

Today, most countries rely on a mix of both kinds of power, often in widely varying amounts depending on their geography and economy. An increasing number of nations are working to diversify their supply and build a considerably more sustainable mix by adding a larger share of renewable sources with each passing year. Understanding this difference helps citizens, engineers, and leaders make better choices about the long-term future of power.

Humans have used renewable energy for thousands of years, long before the modern term existed. Ancient water wheels used the steady power of flowing rivers to grind grain into flour, while sailing ships harnessed the wind to cross oceans and seas, well before coal and oil became widely used fuels during the industrial era that began only a few centuries ago, showing that the search for sustainable power is far older than many people realize.

versions.title: Renewable vs Nonrenewable Energy
versions.text:
Power sources that run nearly every part of modern daily life generally fall into two broad groups, and understanding the difference between them matters more today than arguably ever before, as lights, cars, tools, and machines all depend on a continuous and thoroughly reliable supply of power simply to operate.

The first group, renewable energy, comes from natural sources that continually and dependably replenish on an ordinary human timescale, and these particular sources are therefore considered essentially inexhaustible for all genuinely practical purposes. Sunlight, wind, and flowing water are the most common and widely used renewable sources. The sun predictably rises again every single day without fail, wind keeps circulating across the land in all seasons, and rivers persistently flow toward the sea no matter how much power people ultimately capture from them.

The second group, nonrenewable energy, includes oil, coal, and gas, grouped together under the widely recognized term fossil fuels. These strictly finite fuels formed deep underground over many millions of years, as old plants and animals were gradually and relentlessly transformed by intense heat and immense geological pressure acting over almost unimaginably long stretches of geological time. Because this entirely natural process takes such an extraordinarily long span of time to occur, once a supply of oil, coal, or gas becomes fully and irreversibly used up, people cannot realistically produce any meaningful new supplies within a single lifetime, so for all practical purposes, the supply remains fixed and strictly finite.

A further, equally important distinction separates these two broad groups just as clearly: burning fossil fuels to make usable power releases gases that pollute the air and gradually affect the climate, whereas making power instead from sunlight, wind, and water releases much less of this harmful dirt overall, even after carefully counting the resources needed to build and properly install the equipment.

Today, most countries around the world rely simultaneously on a mix of both kinds of power, often in widely varying amounts depending heavily on their particular geography, climate, and economy. An increasing number of nations are gradually and deliberately working to diversify their overall supply and steadily build a considerably more sustainable mix by adding a larger share of renewable sources with each passing year. Understanding this difference helps citizens, engineers, and leaders alike make better, far more informed choices about the long-term collective future of power.

Humans have actually used renewable energy for many thousands of years, long before the modern term itself ever existed. Ancient water wheels reliably used the steady power of flowing rivers to grind grain into flour, while early sailing ships skillfully harnessed the wind to cross vast oceans and seas, well before coal and oil ever became widely used fuels during the industrial era that began only a relatively few centuries ago, clearly showing that humanity's search for sustainable, dependable power is far older than many people today actually realize.

I used linking words such as first, next, and because.
MID.modelAnswer: Renewable energy, like sunlight, wind, and moving water, comes from sources that naturally replenish themselves and do not run out, because the sun keeps rising and rivers keep flowing. Nonrenewable energy, like oil, coal, and natural gas, formed over millions of years from ancient plants and animals, so once it is used up, people cannot quickly make more of it. This difference matters because burning fossil fuels can pollute the air, while using renewable sources usually creates much less pollution.

keyWords.definition: having a limited amount or size
keyWords.example: The number of seats on the bus is finite, so some riders must stand.

keyWords.definition: able to be continued for a long time without running out or causing serious harm
keyWords.example: Rotating which fields are planted each year is a sustainable farming method.

keyWords.definition: to add different kinds of something instead of relying on just one
keyWords.example: The school decided to diversify its lunch menu with more fruit choices.

keyWords.definition: related to the rocks, layers, and slow processes of the Earth
keyWords.example: Scientists studied the cliff's geological layers to learn its age.
Many people once believed ocean fish were an inexhaustible resource.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Renewable energy sources naturally replenish themselves, while nonrenewable fossil fuels are finite and took millions of years to form.
Fossil fuels will never run out, because nature makes new coal, oil and gas every single year in huge amounts.
Wind and solar power are the same source of energy, since both of them come from burning materials in a furnace.
Each nation currently relies on one main energy source, which is the same for most countries on Earth, and other kinds of energy are rarely used.
questions.why: The article's central comparison is between renewable sources that replenish and finite fossil fuels that took millions of years to form.

wrong.B: The article says fossil fuel supplies are finite and can run out.
wrong.C: Wind and solar are both renewable, but they are different sources.
wrong.D: The article says most nations rely on a mixture of sources.

questions.stem: According to the article, how long does it take for fossil fuels to form underground?
options: A few decades
About one hundred years
Millions of years
A single lifetime
questions.why: The article states that fossil fuels form over the course of millions of years.

wrong.A: A few decades is far too short.
wrong.B: One hundred years is far too short.
wrong.D: A single lifetime is far too short.

questions.stem: What term does the article use to describe oil, coal, and natural gas together?
options: Renewable sources
Fossil fuels
Solar resources
Hydropower
questions.why: The article groups oil, coal, and natural gas together as fossil fuels.

wrong.A: These are described as nonrenewable, not renewable.
wrong.C: Solar resources refers to sunlight, not these fuels.
wrong.D: Hydropower refers to moving water, not these fuels.

questions.stem: The article describes fossil fuel supplies as finite. What does finite mean?
options: Unlimited and endless
Extremely clean
Found only underwater
Limited in amount
questions.why: Finite means limited, which is why fossil fuel supplies can run out.

wrong.A: Finite means the opposite of unlimited.
wrong.B: Cleanliness is not what finite describes.
wrong.C: Location underwater is not what finite describes.

questions.stem: Why does the article call renewable sources "essentially inexhaustible"?
options: Because they were discovered very recently by scientists in a laboratory in a few countries
Because they replenish naturally and are unlikely to run out on a human timescale
Because they formed millions of years ago in the ground, under the sea
Because they cannot be used to generate electricity, said the writer
questions.why: Renewable sources are called inexhaustible because they keep replenishing on a human timescale.

wrong.A: When they were discovered is not discussed.
wrong.C: Forming over millions of years describes fossil fuels, not renewable sources.
wrong.D: The article discusses renewable sources being used to generate energy.

questions.stem: Why might a country with little sunlight or wind still choose to use some fossil fuels?
options: Because its renewable resources may be limited by its geography
Because fossil fuels never pollute the air
Because fossil fuels replenish themselves daily
Because sunlight is available equally in each country on the planet
questions.why: A country's geography can limit how much sunlight or wind it has available to capture.

wrong.B: The article says burning fossil fuels pollutes the air.
wrong.C: Fossil fuels are nonrenewable and do not replenish daily.
wrong.D: The article implies renewable availability can vary by place.

questions.stem: Why does the article suggest nations are diversifying their energy mix?
options: To make fossil fuels form faster
To stop using electricity completely
To increase the number of fossil fuels available in the world
To reduce pollution and rely less on a finite resource
questions.why: Diversifying toward more renewable sources reduces pollution and dependence on a limited resource.

wrong.A: Diversifying does not speed up fossil fuel formation.
wrong.B: The article does not suggest stopping electricity use.
wrong.C: Diversifying adds renewable sources, not more fossil fuels.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe ancient water wheels and sailing ships?
options: To prove that ships are faster than cars
To argue that water wheels are still the best technology
To show that using renewable energy is not a new idea
To explain how modern engines are built
questions.why: The article uses this history to show that people have used renewable energy for thousands of years.

wrong.A: Speed comparisons are not discussed.
wrong.B: The article does not argue water wheels are the best technology today.
wrong.D: Modern engines are not explained.

HIGH.prompt: Should your country invest more in renewable energy, even though it still depends on fossil fuels today? Take a position and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe my country should invest more in renewable energy, even though it still depends on fossil fuels today. One piece of evidence is that fossil fuels are finite, since they take millions of years to form underground, meaning the current supply cannot be replaced once it runs out. Another piece of evidence is that burning fossil fuels pollutes the air and affects the climate, while sunlight, wind, and water generally create far less pollution. Because renewable sources are both essentially inexhaustible and cleaner, investing in them would make my country's energy future more sustainable.

LOW.stem: Where did oil, coal, and gas form?
options: Far up in the sky
Deep underground
Far out in the sea
On top of tall hills
LOW.why: In the text, these fuels formed deep in the ground over millions of years.

wrong.A: The sky is not named.
wrong.C: The sea is not named.
wrong.D: Hills are not named.

LOW.stem: In the article, what does "nonrenewable" mean?
options: It can run out
It never runs out
It is very clean
It is very new
LOW.why: The text says the other kind can run out and calls it nonrenewable.

wrong.B: That describes renewable energy.
wrong.C: Nonrenewable fuels can make the air bad.
wrong.D: These fuels are not new; they formed long ago.

LOW.stem: How is the sun different from oil?
options: Oil never runs out; the sun can
The sun never runs out; oil can
Both of them can run out
Both of them never run out
LOW.why: The sun is renewable and never runs out, while oil is nonrenewable and can run out.

wrong.A: This reverses the two.
wrong.C: The sun does not run out.
wrong.D: Oil can run out.

LOW.stem: Why might a land want to use more sun, wind, and water power some day?
options: It makes the air bad
It costs a lot of fuel
It will run out soon
It keeps the air clean
LOW.why: The text says the sun, wind, and water keep the air clean and never run out.

wrong.A: Burning fuels makes the air bad, not these.
wrong.B: These sources are not fuels.
wrong.C: The text says they never run out.

MID.stem: What were fossil fuels formed from?
options: Old plants and animals
Rivers and large rocks
Wind and bright sunlight
Clocks and simple tools
MID.why: In the text, old plants and animals were slowly changed by heat.

wrong.B: Rivers are renewable, not the source of fossil fuels.
wrong.C: Wind and sunlight are renewable sources.
wrong.D: Clocks and tools use energy but are not its source.

MID.stem: In the article, what does the word "pollute" mean?
options: To make clean
To make dirty
To make quiet
To make bright
MID.why: Burning fossil fuels lets out gases that can pollute the air, which means make it dirty.

wrong.A: Pollute is the opposite of making clean.
wrong.C: Sound is not discussed.
wrong.D: Light is not the point.

MID.stem: How do renewable and nonrenewable power differ in the dirt they let out?
options: Both let out the same dirt
Renewable lets out far less
Nonrenewable lets out far less
Neither one lets out dirt
MID.why: In the text, power from sunlight, wind, and water lets out far less dirt than burning fossil fuels.

wrong.A: The text says they are different.
wrong.C: This reverses the two.
wrong.D: Fossil fuels let out gases that pollute.

MID.stem: Why can people not make more oil, coal, or gas soon?
options: It takes millions of years
It needs a lot of strong wind
The sun does not shine
Rivers have dried up
MID.why: The text says fossil fuels formed over millions of years, so new supplies cannot be made soon.

wrong.B: Wind is a renewable source, not part of making fossil fuels.
wrong.C: The sun is not part of this reason.
wrong.D: Rivers are not part of this reason.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, what changed old plants and animals into fossil fuels?
options: Cold winds and heavy rain
Heat and deep pressure
Sunlight and ocean waves
Rivers and farm tools
HIGH.why: The text says they were transformed by intense heat and geological pressure.

wrong.A: Cold winds are not named.
wrong.C: Sunlight and waves are not named.
wrong.D: Rivers and tools are not named.

HIGH.stem: In the second paragraph, what does the word "persistently" mean?
options: Stopping and starting
Going on and on
Moving very slowly
Moving in circles
HIGH.why: Rivers persistently flow toward the sea, meaning they keep flowing without stopping.

wrong.A: The rivers do not stop and start.
wrong.C: Speed is not the meaning.
wrong.D: They flow toward the sea.

HIGH.stem: Why can people not produce new fossil fuel supplies within a lifetime?
options: Fuels can only be made by hand
Wind carries the fuels far away
Forming them takes a very long time
Rivers wash all the fuels to sea
HIGH.why: The text says this takes such an extraordinarily long span of time that supplies are fixed.

wrong.A: The text says nothing about making fuels by hand.
wrong.B: Wind is not part of this reason.
wrong.D: Rivers are not part of this reason.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author ask where power comes from at the end of the first paragraph?
options: To lead into two groups
To say power has no sources
To end the article early
To talk only about cars
HIGH.why: The question sets up the next paragraphs, which explain renewable and nonrenewable sources.

wrong.B: The article names many sources.
wrong.C: The article continues after the question.
wrong.D: Cars are only one example.
